subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Rabies is a fatal viral encephalitis that spreads from bite wounds to the nervous system. Early post‑exposure prophylaxis saves lives, but once symptoms appear, the disease is almost always lethal.

sections.p: Rabies is an acute, progressive, invariably fatal encephalitis caused by a neurotropic RNA virus of the Lyssavirus genus. It is a global public health problem, especially in rural, low‑resource settings.
The virus is a bullet‑shaped, enveloped particle with a glycoprotein spike that binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on neurons, enabling entry and retrograde transport.

Transmission occurs via saliva from a bite or scratch. After inoculation, the virus replicates at the entry site, travels along peripheral nerves to the spinal cord and brain, then spreads systemically.
b: Bite or scratch is most common

t.b: Detects viral RNA at source; positive confirms exposure
Assesses post‑exposure prophylaxis response; >0.5 IU/mL considered protective

sections.p: Clinical progression follows a prodromal phase (fever, malaise) to a furious or paralytic phase. Once neurological signs appear, mortality is >99%.
Diagnosis is clinical once neurological signs appear. Laboratory confirmation is by detecting viral antigen or RNA in saliva, CSF, or skin biopsy.
Post‑exposure prophylaxis (PEP) with wound cleaning, rabies immunoglobulin, and a series of inactivated vaccine doses is curative if started promptly. No effective treatment exists after onset.
b: Supportive care: airway protection, seizure control

t.b: Reduces viral load at inoculation site; essential before PEP
Completion within 14 days is critical for protection

sections.p: Remember the ‘bite‑to‑brain’ timeline: 1–3 days prodrome, 2–5 days furious phase, 2–7 days paralytic phase. PEP must be started within 24 h of exposure.
b: Hydrophobia is a hallmark of furious rabies

sections.p: Other causes of encephalitis (HSV, Japanese encephalitis) and neuroleptic malignant syndrome can mimic rabies, but the history of bite and rapid progression help differentiate.
b: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability

sections.p: Early CSF may be normal; skin biopsy can be falsely negative if taken too early. Antibody titres may be low if PEP was incomplete.

whenToSeekHelp: Any bite from a wild or stray animal, especially if the animal is acting strangely; any neurological signs such as agitation, hydrophobia, or paralysis after a bite

faq.q: Can rabies be prevented after a bite?
faq.a: Yes, if post‑exposure prophylaxis is started promptly and completed, it is almost 100% effective.
No, human‑to‑human transmission is extremely rare and only occurs in organ transplantation or laboratory exposure.

faq.q: What is the most common animal source in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Dogs, especially free‑roaming or stray dogs, are responsible for >95% of human cases.

exam: Explain why post‑exposure prophylaxis is effective only if started before symptom onset.
Describe the pathogenesis of rabies virus neurotropism and its clinical implications.
Outline the diagnostic workup for a patient with suspected rabies in a setting without PCR capability.
